rv: First of all, some of comments were by film illiterates. Republic Pictures was NOT a poverty row studio. It was owned by Herbert J. Yates, who happened to also own CFI, Consolidated Film Industries, the main film laboratory in Hollywood. That is, CFI processed the films of the "major" studios. Indeed, Yates was a businessman who owned CFI and figured since he had the lab he would start a studio himself--Republic Pictures. Yates was a good bottom line businessman. He bought up a string of smaller companies to form Republic. He KNEW what kind of movies people liked simply from the amount of…

The credits announce that this film "introduces" Gene Autry but Autry's first film was actually "In Old Santa Fe" (1934). Boy meets girl. Boy seems to lose girl. Boy finds girl again. A timeless plot line that still works. Very entertaining performances by all.

Although I agree that this film has problems, it also has much to recommend it. Ted Lewis, Kay Thompson, and Cab Calloway were true American originals and Phil Regan was a good singer. The settings, probably borrowed, were lavish and of course Miss Dvorak turned in her usual fine performance. And a rare chance to see Tamara Geva, what more should we expect from a Poverty Row studio?

rv: Excerpt from a longer movie- it’s a Cautionary Tale

From Wikipedia- Is Your Daughter Safe (1927) was one of the earliest exploitation films in which nudity appeared. A compilation of medical documentary films and stock footage of nude scenes dating back to the 1900s, it was presented as an educational film about the dangers of venereal disease, white slavery, and prostitution. Exploitation short subjects (three to 15 minutes in length) with comedic plots and frequent nudity were also produced in the silent era. The movie was renamed The Octopus because of social pressures.

This was released in 1927, but much of the nude footage is closer to the 1900s. A compilation of nude scenes and medical films edited together and presented as a cautionary tale regarding VD, white slavery, prostitution, etc. Perhaps the first "white coater" pseudo-educational film of its kind.

Judging by the final frame, this was meant to be a trailer for a longer film, "the most sensational film of the year." Today the film work would be considered amateurish, but at the time it was made it may have been as good as it got. It looks like a semi-legal "stag film" of its era. Three stars for curiosity value.

These rather portly girls definitely don't fit the strict body shapes of today, and that does make this film stand out. The ladies mostly pose on rocks, hardly erotic and mostly arty. Good on them though for being so brave and free thinking at that time. The end credit I'm presuming is just a dumb edit from some guffawing film editor wanting to have a laugh.

Although this film is stated to be from 1927, it appears to be from a much earlier time. This is understandable when you see the last frame,, which says "A Millard Production". this would be S.S. This movie has a TON of home movie goodness crammed into it it's so hard to describe, filmed (I think?) in lovely Kodachrome, this has vibrant crisp colors in it that makes it a joy to watch from beginning to end. Highlights include the girl swinging on the bars in scene #1! The amazing recreations of musical scenes from movies (or maybe plays!). These were silent, anyone know what these were? The amazing shots on the waterfront and the trip to Coronado. Very nice, highly reccomended!
